name: George Washington Carver
title: George Washington Carver: learning to serve those who work the land
description: Scientist and educator George Washington Carver connected his faith with a life of study and service in the face of the barriers of racial discrimination.

sections.heading: Seeking an education despite the barriers
paragraphs: George Washington Carver was born into slavery in Missouri near the end of the American Civil War. His search for an education took him to several towns. He faced obstacles because of his origins and because of racial discrimination; one school even withdrew his admission when it learned he was Black.

He studied at Simpson College and then at Iowa State, where he earned a master of science degree in 1896. Artistic training and an interest in plants were part of his journey. Later he worked at Tuskegee, an institution devoted to educating African American students.

sections.heading: Knowledge that could reach the farm
paragraphs: At Tuskegee he taught farming practices, among them crop rotation and the use of alternatives to cotton. His work sought to improve farmers’ opportunities. Research and teaching thus met questions about the land, food, and a family’s livelihood.

The National Park Service preserves an autobiographical account in which Carver connects his perseverance with trust in God. His faith was part of the way he understood his life. He died in 1943, after a long career as a scientist and educator.

reflection: Colossians 3:23–24 calls us to work with all our heart, as before the Lord. Carver’s story helps us think about work that joins preparation with attention to our neighbor’s needs. Studying carefully and sharing what we have learned can be forms of service in a classroom, on a farm, or in a workshop.

One person’s perseverance does not remove the responsibility to confront the discrimination he suffered. A Christian community can open up opportunities to learn, recognize the work of others, and stand by those who meet unjust barriers. Faith also shows itself in the way we treat and value the people we work alongside.
review_note: An approximate birth date is used, given the historical uncertainty. Carver is not credited with inventing peanut butter, and popular figures for his inventions are not included.
